young.html: When one billiard ball hits another, the second one rolls away. You knew that would happen. But how did you know? David Hume, a Scottish thinker, asked this question and gave a surprising answer.

Hume said we never actually see one ball make the other move. We see ball one move, we see the touch, and we see ball two move. That's all. After seeing this many times, our mind gets used to it and expects it. Hume called this habit custom.
So we learn about the world only by experience, and custom is "the great guide of human life." It works very well. But Hume said it is a habit, not a proof.

young.name: gb-billiards
young.cap: Strike the ball and watch. Each time, count what you actually see. Do you ever see the push itself?

young.html: Guess what happens. Show a child something they have never seen: a magnet near a paper clip, or baking soda dropped in vinegar (with a grown-up). Before doing it, ask them to guess what will happen. Could they know without ever having seen it? Then do it twice more. Notice how quickly we start to expect it.

full.html: Hume (1711–1776) first put his ideas in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40), which, he said, "fell dead-born from the press." He rewrote the first part more briefly and clearly as An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748). He also wrote a bestselling History of England and essays on politics and economics, and was a close friend of Adam Smith.

Hume divides what is in the mind into impressions, our lively perceptions when we see, hear, feel or want, and ideas, their fainter copies in memory and thought. Every simple idea comes from an impression. So to test a puzzling idea, ask: from what impression is it copied? If none, the word may have no meaning.

All reasoning, Hume says, is about one of two things. Relations of ideas, such as "three times five is half of thirty," are known by thought alone; denying them is a contradiction. Matters of fact, such as "the sun will rise tomorrow," are known only by experience; their opposite is always conceivable.

head: Relations of ideas
Matters of fact
rows: the sun will rise; fire burns; bread nourishes

full.html: All our reasoning about matters of fact rests on cause and effect. But where does that idea come from? Not from reason alone:

full.text: When I see, for instance, a Billiard-ball moving in a straight line towards another; even suppose motion in the second ball should by accident be suggested to me, as the result of their contact or impulse; may I not conceive, that a hundred different events might as well follow from that cause? May not both these balls remain at absolute rest? May not the first ball return in a straight line, or leap off from the second in any line or direction? All these suppositions are consistent and conceivable.
full.author: David Hume
full.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

full.html: Nor from a single experience, since we see only one event following another, never a hidden power or "necessary connexion" between them. Even after many experiences, reasoning can't prove that the future will resemble the past, because any argument for that would already assume it. What carries us from past to future is custom:

full.text: Custom, then, is the great guide of human life. It is that principle alone which renders our experience useful to us, and makes us expect, for the future, a similar train of events with those which have appeared in the past.
full.author: David Hume
full.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

full.name: gb-billiards
full.cap: The idea of cause, in Hume's terms: contact, one event after another, and a constant conjunction we have seen many times. Count the trials, and notice what you never see.

full.html: In Section X Hume argues that testimony for a miracle, a violation of a law of nature, must be weighed against all the uniform experience that established that law; a wise person proportions belief to the evidence. Religious readers have answered this argument from his day to ours, and it remains one of the most debated pages he wrote.

Hume did not want people to stop believing in the world. Nature, he said, is too strong for that. He recommends a mitigated skepticism: modest, careful, and limited to subjects our minds can handle. He ends with a famous, sharp test for books:

full.text: If we take in our hand any volume; of divinity or school metaphysics, for instance; let us ask, Does it contain any abstract reasoning concerning quantity or number? No. Does it contain any experimental reasoning concerning matter of fact and existence? No. Commit it then to the flames: for it can contain nothing but sophistry and illusion.
full.author: David Hume
full.ed: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, reprinted from the edition of 1777, Open Court, Chicago

full.html: Thinking Hume said causes don't exist. He said we can't prove by reason that causes must work the same way tomorrow, and that our idea of cause comes from constant conjunction and custom. He relied on causal reasoning in everything he did.

deep.html: Philosophers call Hume's puzzle about the future "the problem of induction." Kant said Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber" and wrote the Critique of Pure Reason partly in answer. In the 20th century some philosophers argued that science advances by testing and trying to refute guesses rather than proving them, while others defend probability-based accounts of how evidence supports theories. No answer has satisfied everyone.

Thomas Reid, another Scot, argued that Hume's starting point, that we know only our own impressions and ideas, leads to absurd results, and that common sense beliefs deserve trust. Defenders of miracles, from George Campbell in Hume's day onward, argued that his test sets the bar so that no testimony could ever be enough. Hume's admirers answer that he asks only for evidence in proportion to the claim.
